entry: [[Chemical element]] with symbol Eu and atomic number 63, a soft, silvery-white [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] metal that is the most chemically reactive of the lanthanides. Because the metal is effectively divalent, it has an unusually low density and large atomic volume for a lanthanide. Its density is about 5.24 g/cm³ and it melts at 822 °C (1,095 K). Europium occurs in nature only as a minor component of [[Rare-earth element|rare-earth]] minerals. Its +2 state lets it enter [[Feldspar|feldspar]], producing europium anomalies used in [[Petrology|petrology]]. Eugène-Anatole Demarçay reported evidence for it in 1896, associated with [[Samarium|samarium]], and named it after [[Europe]] in 1901, when he obtained it in pure form. Europium phosphors became important in color television in the 1960s and remain key to lighting and [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diodes]]. It has no known biological role, and the pyrophoric metal must be protected from air and moisture.

High-speed rail service in Western Europe, connecting Belgium, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom through the [[Channel Tunnel]]. Eurostar Group, which operates the service, was formed from the merger of Eurostar and Thalys. Services began on November 14, 1994, and more than 400 million passengers have traveled on them, including a record 20 million in 2025. Since 1998 the service has won multiple World Travel Awards.

Annual international song competition organized since 1956 by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Each participating broadcaster submits an original song, performed live, and countries award points to their favorite songs to determine a winner. The contest has been held every year since 1956 except 2020, due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], and is the longest-running international music competition on television. Broadcasters from 52 countries have taken part at least once. Ireland and Sweden have won the most, with seven victories each, and Germany has competed in all but one edition. Former performers include [[ABBA]], Céline Dion, [[Cliff Richard]] and [[Julio Iglesias]]. Critics have argued that political allegiances between countries may influence the results.

Extinct order of marine [[Arthropod|arthropods]], informally called sea scorpions. The earliest known eurypterids date to the Tremadocian stage of the Ordovician period, about 480 million years ago. With approximately 250 species, the order is the most diverse Paleozoic chelicerate order. Eurypterids were major components of [[Silurian]] marine faunas, and the genus *Eurypterus* accounts for more than 90% of known specimens. Only the earliest forms were marine; many later eurypterids lived in brackish or fresh water and were not true [[Scorpion|scorpions]]. The order includes the largest known arthropods, *Jaekelopterus*, at 2.5 m (8.2 ft) long. Their extinction is dated either to the early Middle [[Permian]] or to the [[Permian–Triassic extinction event]], 251.9 million years ago.

Christian bishop and historian from the Roman province of Syria Palaestina, known as the "Father of Church history." In about AD 314 he became bishop of Caesarea Palaestina. A scholar of the biblical canon, he is regarded as one of the most learned Christians of [[Late antiquity|late antiquity]]. His works include the *Ecclesiastical History*, the *Chronicle* and *On the Martyrs*, along with studies of the biblical text such as *Demonstrations of the Gospel* and *On Discrepancies between the Gospels*. His *Onomasticon* is an early geographical lexicon of places in the Holy Land mentioned in the Bible. He also wrote a biographical work on [[Constantine the Great]], the first Christian Roman emperor, who was Augustus between AD 306 and AD 337.

Practice of intentionally ending life to eliminate [[Pain|pain]] and [[Suffering|suffering]]. Laws differ between countries. Euthanasia is classified as voluntary, when a person wishes to die; non-voluntary, when a patient's consent is unavailable, as in a [[Vegetative state|persistent vegetative state]] or [[Coma|coma]]; and involuntary, when done against a patient's will, which is illegal in all countries and usually considered [[Murder|murder]]. Passive euthanasia, or "pulling the plug," is legal under some circumstances in many countries. Active euthanasia is legal or de facto legal in only a handful of countries, including [[Belgium]], [[Canada]] and [[Uruguay]], where it is limited to specific circumstances. As of 2006, euthanasia had become the most active area of research in bioethics.

German photographer and longtime companion of [[Adolf Hitler]]. She met Hitler in [[Munich]] in 1929, when she was 17 and working for his photographer, Heinrich Hoffmann. From 1936 she was part of his household at the Berghof, near Berchtesgaden. In 1945 she went to [[Berlin]] to be with him in the Führerbunker, where they married on April 29, 1945. Both died by suicide less than 40 hours later; Braun took [[Cyanide|cyanide]]. Much of the public did not know of the relationship until after their deaths. Braun created many of the surviving color photographs and films of Hitler.

American actress, producer, director and businesswoman. She gained popularity as Gabrielle Solis in the ABC series [[Desperate Housewives]] (2004–2012), a role that earned her two Screen Actors Guild Awards and a Golden Globe nomination. In 2005 she founded the production company UnbeliEVAble Entertainment. Her directorial work includes the Oscar-nominated film *Flamin' Hot* (2023). She received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2018.

American actress whose career spanned seven decades. Her film debut in [[Elia Kazan|Elia Kazan]]'s *On the Waterfront* (1954), opposite [[Marlon Brando]], won her an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Supporting Actress. She later played Eve Kendall in [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s *North by Northwest* (1959). Her Primetime Emmy Award came for the miniseries *People Like Us* (1990), and she received two stars on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]]. At the time of her death she was one of the oldest living Academy Award winners.

Argentine politician and activist who served as First Lady of Argentina from 1946 to 1952, as the wife of President [[Juan Perón]]. Born into poverty in the [[Pampas]], she became a central figure of Peronism. She championed [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]] in Argentina, founded the Eva Perón Foundation and the Female Peronist Party, and ran the Ministries of Labor and Health. In 1951 she withdrew her candidacy for vice president amid opposition from the military and the [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]], and her declining health. After her death she was given a state funeral, a prerogative generally reserved for heads of state.

American businessman, co-founder and [[Chief executive officer|chief executive]] of Snap Inc. Born in [[Los Angeles]], he proposed an ephemeral messaging app as a product design class project at [[Stanford University]] in 2011. With Stanford classmates Bobby Murphy and Reggie Brown, he developed a prototype called Picaboo, which was renamed [[Snapchat]]. He was the youngest billionaire in the world in 2015. As of August 2025, his personal net worth was $2.5 billion according to [[Forbes]].

American former professional boxer and the only four-time world heavyweight champion. He won a bronze medal in the light heavyweight division at the 1984 Summer Olympics and competed professionally between 1984 and 2011. He was undisputed cruiserweight champion in the late 1980s and won the unified heavyweight titles in 1990 by defeating Buster Douglas. In 1996 he defeated [[Mike Tyson]] to become the first boxer since [[Muhammad Ali]] to win a world heavyweight title three times. Nicknamed "the Real Deal," he was known for his resilience in the ring.

Worldwide interdenominational movement within [[Protestantism|Protestant]] Christianity that emphasizes evangelism and personal conversion, often described as being "born again." Evangelicals regard the [[Bible]] as the ultimate authority in matters of faith and practice. The movement's roots lie in the [[Reformation]] of the 16th century, and the modern movement is generally dated to around 1734. It gained momentum in the First Great Awakening of the 1730s and 1740s, with figures such as [[John Wesley]] and George Whitefield. Evangelicalism is found in many Protestant denominations, including [[Baptists]], [[Methodism]] and [[Quakers]]. The World Evangelical Alliance claims 600 million believers in 2025, roughly one in four Christians. Some critics argue that the term covers such a wide range of beliefs that it is difficult to define as a unified movement.

Canadian actress and author. She gained popularity as Kate Austen in the ABC drama *Lost*, which garnered her six Saturn Award nominations for Best Actress on Television. She played Tauriel in Peter Jackson's *The Hobbit* films, *The Desolation of Smaug* (2013) and *The Battle of the Five Armies* (2014). She has since portrayed Hope van Dyne / Wasp in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]]. She is also the author of the children's book series *The Squickerwonkers*.

Vaporization that occurs on the surface of a [[Liquid|liquid]] as it changes into the gas phase. Molecules near the surface that gain enough [[Kinetic energy|kinetic energy]] to overcome the vapor pressure escape into the air. Because the most energetic [[Molecule|molecules]] leave, the remaining liquid cools, a process called evaporative cooling; this is why evaporating sweat cools the human body. Evaporation proceeds faster at higher [[Temperature|temperatures]] and in liquids with higher vapor pressure, but it slows when the surrounding air already holds a high concentration of the evaporating substance. In an enclosed space, evaporation continues until the vapor is saturated and the rate of return equals the rate of escape. Evaporation is an essential part of the [[Water cycle|water cycle]], as the sun drives evaporation from oceans, lakes and soil. In [[Hydrology|hydrology]], evaporation and [[Transpiration|transpiration]] together are termed evapotranspiration.

American stunt performer known for more than 75 ramp-to-ramp motorcycle jumps. Born in [[Montana|Butte, Montana]], he gained international fame after a 1967 attempt to jump the fountains at Caesars Palace in [[Las Vegas]] ended in a severe crash. In 1974 his rocket-powered Skycycle X-2 failed to cross the Snake River Canyon in [[Idaho]] after the parachute deployed prematurely. Ideal Toy Company sold over $125 million worth of Knievel toys from 1972 to 1977. After an assault conviction and jail time, he declared bankruptcy. He died of [[Diabetes|diabetes]] and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Boundary in spacetime beyond which no signal can ever reach a given observer, a concept in [[Astrophysics|astrophysics]]. Wolfgang Rindler coined the term in the 1950s. In 1784, John Michell proposed that a massive compact object could have an [[Escape velocity|escape velocity]] greater than the [[Speed of light|speed of light]], so that light would fall back. In 1958, David Finkelstein used [[General relativity|general relativity]] to define a stricter event horizon for a [[Black hole|black hole]], beyond which events of any kind cannot affect an outside observer. [[Stephen Hawking|Stephen Hawking]] later suggested using an apparent horizon instead, arguing that "Gravitational collapse produces apparent horizons but no event horizons." A cosmic event horizon affects all kinds of signals, including [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]].

Natural region of flooded grasslands in southern [[Florida]], forming the southern half of the Kissimmee-Okeechobee-Everglades watershed. The system begins near Orlando with the Kissimmee River, which discharges into the shallow Lake Okeechobee. In the wet season, water leaving the lake forms a slow-moving river 60 miles (97 km) wide that flows south across a [[Limestone|limestone]] shelf to Florida Bay. In 1947 Congress formed the Central and Southern Florida Flood Control Project, which built 1,400 miles (2,300 km) of canals and levees. About 50 percent of the original Everglades has been developed as agricultural or urban land, and the primary crop was [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]]. [[UNESCO]] and the Ramsar Convention designated the Everglades a Wetland Area of Global Importance. In 2000 Congress approved the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan.

Body of facts in a legal proceeding, and the rules that govern their proof. The rules determine what the trier of fact, a judge or [[Jury|jury]], may consider, and how much proof of what quality is needed to prevail. Standards range from reasonable suspicion to preponderance of the evidence, clear and convincing evidence, and beyond a reasonable doubt. Key admissibility rules concern hearsay, [[Authentication|authentication]], relevance, privilege, [[Witness|witnesses]], [[Opinion|opinions]], expert testimony and identification. Rules vary between criminal, civil and family [[Court|courts]] and across jurisdictions. English [[Common law|common law]] developed many of them after juries became central in the 16th and 17th centuries, including a prohibition on hearsay.

Theoretical approach in [[Psychology|psychology]] that examines [[Cognition|cognition]] and behavior from an evolutionary perspective. It seeks to identify human psychological [[Adaptation|adaptations]] that evolved to solve ancestral problems, such as food choices, social hierarchies, and selecting mates. Its central assumption is that the brain consists of specialized mechanisms shaped by [[Natural selection|natural selection]], although some traits are non-adaptive by-products of adaptive ones. Traits found in all cultures, such as inferring others' emotions, recognizing kin and cooperating, are considered good candidates for adaptations. Its ideas are applied in [[Economics|economics]], law, management, [[Psychiatry|psychiatry]], [[Politics|politics]] and [[Literature|literature]]. Critics question its testability and its assumptions about the ancestral environment.

Scottish actor and filmmaker. He gained international recognition as the drug addict Mark Renton in *Trainspotting* (1996) and as Obi-Wan Kenobi in the *Star Wars* prequel trilogy (1999–2005). He won a Golden Globe Award for his dual role in the television series *Fargo* (2017) and a Primetime Emmy Award for the miniseries *Halston* (2021). He was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 2013 for his service to drama and charity, and has been an ambassador for [[UNICEF]] UK since 2004.

Educational assessment intended to measure a test-taker's knowledge, skill, aptitude or physical fitness. Tests may be administered verbally, on paper or on a computer, or in an area where the test-taker performs a set of skills. Formal testing often produces a grade or test score, interpreted against a norm or criterion. Informal tests existed throughout history, including archery contests in [[China]] since the [[Zhou dynasty]]. Standardized written examinations were first implemented in China, where the imperial examinations (*keju*) originated in 605 under the [[Sui dynasty]]. The [[Tang dynasty]] expanded them, and [[Wu Zetian]] extensively expanded the system further. During the [[Song dynasty]] the examinations became the primary means of selecting scholar-officials.

Mythical sword of [[King Arthur]], said to have magical powers and to be associated with the rightful [[Sovereignty|sovereignty]] of Britain. Its first reliably datable appearance is in Geoffrey of Monmouth's *Historia Regum Britanniae* (c. 1136), where Arthur's sword is called Caliburnus. The name may derive from the Welsh *Caledfwlch*, a compound of *caled* ("hard") and *bwlch* ("breach, cleft"). In Robert de Boron's *Merlin*, the sword in the stone proves Arthur's lineage. In Thomas Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur*, a different sword from the Lady of the Lake shares the name.

Obsolete, paraphyletic group of unicellular [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], first suggested by Simpson and Patterson in 1999 and given a rank by Thomas Cavalier-Smith in 2002. Its name refers to the excavated appearance of a ventral feeding groove. Most excavates are unicellular, heterotrophic [[Flagellate|flagellates]] with two, four or more flagella, and only some [[Euglenozoa|euglenozoans]] are photosynthetic. Many lack classical [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]], and some anaerobic intestinal parasites have greatly reduced them. The group includes human parasites such as *Giardia* and *Trichomonas*. Phylogenomic analyses show that it contains three widely separated groups: discobids, metamonads and malawimonads. The [[Slime mold|slime molds]] of the family Acrasidae are the only excavates with limited multicellularity.

Rate at which one [[Currency|currency]] is exchanged for another, reflecting the value of one country's currency in relation to another. Currencies may be national, sub-national like [[Hong Kong]], or supra-national like the [[Euro]]. For example, an interbank rate of 141 [[Japanese yen]] to the [[United States dollar]] means that ¥141 buys US$1. Each country determines its exchange rate regime, which may be floating, pegged or a hybrid. In floating regimes, rates are set in the foreign exchange market, which trades 24 hours a day except weekends. Money dealers at [[Bank|banks]] and bureaux de change quote separate buying and selling rates, and the difference is the bid–ask spread.
